common_name: Melrose Pepper (Utica-Style Italian-American Heirloom Frying Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Melrose is an Italian-American heirloom frying pepper long grown by home gardeners in central New York's Mohawk Valley, producing elongated, thin-walled, pale green fruits that ripen to red with a sweet flavor and only the faintest hint of heat.

directions: Sow seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Melrose is an Italian-American heirloom frying pepper long cultivated by home gardeners in central New York's Mohawk Valley, prized for the elongated, thin-walled, pale green fruits that mature to red and carry a sweet flavor with only the faintest whisper of heat. The tender walls cook down quickly when sautéed in olive oil with garlic, making it the traditional pepper folded into Utica-style braised greens alongside hot cherry peppers, breadcrumbs, and provolone. Pick some pods green for a milder, grassier flavor and let others ripen fully red on the vine for maximum sweetness.

common_name: Quadrato d'Asti Pepper (Piedmontese Blocky Sweet Frying Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Quadrato d'Asti ('square from Asti') is a traditional Piedmontese Italian sweet pepper producing blocky, deeply four-lobed fruits with thick, crisp walls that ripen from green to golden yellow or red.

directions: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks ahead of the last frost, keeping soil warm for even germination, then transplant once frost danger has passed. Quadrato d'Asti ('square from Asti') is a traditional Piedmontese sweet pepper named for its home region in northern Italy, producing blocky, deeply four-lobed fruits with thick, crisp walls that ripen from green to golden yellow or red depending on the strain grown. The dense flesh holds its shape well when roasted, grilled, or stuffed, and the flavor turns notably sweeter and richer as the fruit fully colors. Give plants sturdy support in windy gardens, since the heavy fruit can weigh down brittle branches.

common_name: Boldog Hungarian Spice Paprika Pepper (Heirloom Drying Paprika)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Boldog Hungarian Spice takes its name from the Hungarian town of Boldog, a historic paprika-growing center, and produces compact plants loaded with small, thin-walled, sweet fruits bred specifically for drying and grinding into paprika.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and set plants out once the soil has warmed thoroughly. Boldog Hungarian Spice takes its name from the Hungarian town of Boldog, a historic center of paprika production, and produces compact plants loaded with small, tapering, thin-walled fruits that ripen to a deep brick red. Bred specifically for drying and grinding, the pods carry sweet, richly aromatic flesh with no heat, and their thin walls dry quickly once strung into ristras or dehydrated. The heavy, early fruit set makes it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting to produce their own homemade sweet paprika powder in a single season.

common_name: Mama Mia Giallo Pepper (Early Yellow Italian Frying Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Mama Mia Giallo is a modern Italian frying pepper hybrid bred for earliness and heavy production, bearing slender, tapering fruits that mature from green to glossy golden yellow with thin, sweet, corno-type walls.

directions: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Mama Mia Giallo is a modern Italian frying pepper bred for earliness and productivity, bearing slender, tapering fruits that mature from green to a glossy golden yellow with the thin walls and sweet flavor typical of classic Italian corno-type peppers. Market growers favor it for its ability to set fruit heavily even under cooler, less-than-ideal conditions, giving a longer harvest window than many heirloom frying types. Harvest at the yellow stage for peak sweetness, or pick some pods green for a milder, more vegetal flavor.

common_name: Doux Long des Landes Pepper (French Heirloom Sweet Frying Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Doux Long des Landes is a traditional French heirloom sweet pepper from the Landes region of southwestern France, producing long, tapering, thin-walled fruits that ripen from pale green to red with a mild, sweet flavor.

directions: Sow indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F. Doux Long des Landes is a traditional French sweet pepper named for the Landes region of southwestern France, producing long, tapering, thin-walled fruits that ripen from pale green to red with a mild, sweet flavor and virtually no heat. Its thin flesh makes it well suited to quick pan-frying in oil in the French country style, or to roasting whole until the skin blisters and slips off easily. The plants are productive over a long season and tolerate the warm, humid summers common in the Gulf South.

common_name: Flavorburst Bell Pepper (Color-Changing Purple-to-Orange Sweet Bell Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Flavorburst is a blocky bell-type sweet pepper bred for its unusual ripening sequence, passing from green through deep purple to yellow before finishing at bright orange, an AAS-recognized cultivar prized for both color and sweet flavor.

directions: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed. Flavorburst is a blocky bell-type sweet pepper bred for its unusual ripening sequence, with fruit passing from green through deep purple to yellow before finishing at bright orange, giving multiple colorful harvest stages from a single planting. The thick, crisp walls carry a sweet, mild flavor at every color stage, though sweetness increases as the fruit reaches its final orange color. Because the color changes track ripeness, gardeners can pick fruit at whichever stage suits their taste rather than waiting solely for full color change.
